passage: I'm Samir, and I sit two desks from Reena. For a month I've noticed Reena staying past seven to finish the quarterly deck, then taking a call in the corridor. Reena's parents want to fix a date for a relative's ceremony and expect Reena to travel for the whole week. On Monday, Reena said sorry to the manager, and on Tuesday said sorry to a parent on the phone in nearly the same voice. Reena's eyes looked tired but the smile stayed polite. I can't tell what exactly Reena feels; maybe guilt about both, maybe resentment too. On Friday I heard, “I love them, and I'm also so cross with them,” said to nobody in particular.

Thursday: Sunaina stayed late for the launch, missed the call from her mother, then felt guilty and ordered nothing for dinner.

Sunday: She reached the puja an hour late, left before the prasad, and half-listened during the dinner. She felt guilty about each thing, and a little resentful about all of them, and both feelings sat together in her chest.

passage: Rehana, twenty-five, worked as an auditor in Hyderabad, and March was the busiest month of her year. Her parents wanted her home in Warangal for her cousin's engagement on Sunday. Her sister Mehak called every evening: "Ammi's asking again." Rehana also had a pottery class she'd paid for and hadn't attended in three weeks. On Friday night she sat on her bed with her laptop, a train ticket she hadn't booked, and a text from her manager about Saturday work. She felt guilty toward her parents, guilty toward her work, and underneath it, a flash of resentment she was ashamed of. "Why is it always me who has to choose?" she whispered, and opened the booking site anyway.

qa.q: Where did Rehana's parents want her to come?
qa.a: They wanted her home in Warangal for her cousin's engagement.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Rehana have on Friday night?
qa.a: She felt guilty toward both her parents and her work, and also a flash of resentment she was ashamed of.

qa.q: What could Rehana do to make the choice less painful?
qa.a: She could tell her manager and Mehak honestly what she can manage, perhaps going home for one day and working on Saturday, instead of silently trying to do everything.

qa.q: How might Mehak see Rehana's hesitation?
qa.a: Mehak, passing on Ammi's reminders every evening, might see Rehana as busy or distant, without knowing the guilt and resentment she is carrying.

passage:
Jeevan: "Lakshmi, Amma called again. She wants to know if you're coming for Pongal."
Lakshmi: "I told her I have the product launch that week."
Jeevan: "She says you said that at Diwali too."
Lakshmi: "Because it was true at Diwali too."
Jeevan: "She's getting old. She misses you."
Lakshmi: "Don't you think I know that? I feel terrible every time I say no."
Jeevan: "Then come."
Lakshmi: "And lose the launch? And then my yoga class, my one evening for myself, goes too, like always."
Jeevan: "So you're angry at Amma?"
Lakshmi: "No. Yes. I'm angry at everything wanting me. And I still want to go home."
Jeevan: (quietly) "Can you do two days? I'll tell Amma it's two days."
Lakshmi: "Two days. Okay."

qa.q: What festival does Amma want Lakshmi home for?
qa.a: Amma wants Lakshmi home for Pongal.

qa.q: What is Lakshmi feeling about the invitation?
qa.a: Lakshmi feels guilty about saying no, resentful that everything is pulling at once, and still longs to go home.

qa.q: What helped the conversation move forward?
qa.a: Jeevan's offer of a two-day visit gave Lakshmi a realistic middle path between the launch and family.

qa.q: How does Jeevan see the situation between Lakshmi and Amma?
qa.a: Jeevan is caught in the middle, passing on Amma's hurt, but also tries to find a practical compromise.

grounding: A dialogue shows a young professional feeling both duty and resentment as work, family and personal time collide.

passage: I'm Zubin. At twenty-four I had a job in consulting that swallowed my weeks, parents in Surat who needed me for hospital visits, and a friend, Pankaj, whose wedding I'd promised to help plan. I loved all of them. And I felt guilty about whichever one I was ignoring that day. When I was at work, I thought of Mum's appointments. When I was at the hospital, my phone buzzed with client emails. The worst part was the resentment. Why did I have to carry it all? Then I'd feel ashamed for resenting my own parents. Pankaj noticed first. "You can love them and be tired of it too," he said. That sentence helped.

qa.q: Where did Zubin's parents live?
qa.a: Zubin's parents lived in Surat.

qa.q: What feelings did Zubin carry at the same time?
qa.a: Zubin felt guilty about whichever duty was being ignored, resentful at carrying everything, and then ashamed of that resentment.

qa.q: What could Zubin try next after hearing Pankaj's words?
qa.a: Accept that duty and resentment can sit together, then talk openly with family, work and Pankaj about what can realistically be done each week.

qa.q: How might Pankaj see Zubin during those months?
qa.a: Pankaj seems to notice Zubin's strain before anyone else and responds with understanding rather than asking for more help with the wedding.

grounding: A young professional reflects on work, parents and friendship colliding, and on duty and resentment coexisting.

subtype: Work, family and personal duties colliding [Actor]
passage:
Team lead's note, Friday. Samir.
For three weeks Tanvir has left at six sharp on Tuesdays and Thursdays to drive his parents to his father's physiotherapy, then logged in again at ten at night. On Wednesday he stayed back after stand-up and told me his mother also wants him home every Sunday, and his fiancée has stopped asking when they will look at wedding venues. He said, "Whatever I pick, somebody's let down. Some days I'm angry at all of them, and then I feel terrible for being angry at my own parents." He rubbed his eyes the whole time.
I didn't try to solve his family. I moved the client review from Thursday to Monday and told him late-night logins are not expected. I also said both feelings can be true at once. I'll check in again next Friday.

qa.q: On which days did Tanvir leave at six?
qa.a: On Tuesdays and Thursdays.

qa.q: What mix of feelings does Tanvir describe?
qa.a: He feels guilty whichever duty he neglects, resentful towards everyone pulling at him, and then ashamed of that anger towards his own parents.

qa.q: Which of Samir's steps helped most, and why?
qa.a: Moving the client review and saying late logins are not expected eased real pressure, and saying both feelings can be true lets Tanvir stop fighting himself.

qa.q: How might Tanvir's fiancée be feeling, given that she has stopped asking about venues?
qa.a: She may feel pushed to the bottom of the list and quietly hurt or resigned, as if asking again would only add to his load.

grounding: Shows a young professional torn between a demanding job, his parents' needs and his own relationship, feeling guilt and resentment at once.
